joke.text: Captain, sorry to interrupt. I have a joke here — I am practising. Care to rate it?
Captain, onboard computer online. A fresh entry appeared in the humour log.
Captain, permission to report: a joke detected. It poses no danger.
Captain, while we cruise at speed, how about a minute of laughter?
Captain, the engineers in the engine room told a joke. Relaying on intercom.
Captain, my build passed with zero errors. I will mark that with a joke.
Captain, sensors show crew mood down two percent. Recommending a joke.
Captain, incoming joke from a neighbouring ship. Accept the signal?
Captain, everyone in Neon City is retelling one joke. Want to hear it?
Captain, boiler pressure is nominal. Perfect time for a joke.
Captain, the programmers in bay three have been laughing for ten minutes. I found out why.
Captain, I am training my sense of humour. Another test. Will you listen?
Captain, serious report. Just kidding. It is a joke.
Captain, something funny turned up in the logs. Read it aloud?
Captain, commit of the week: a joke. Needs your review.
Captain, coffee is ready in the galley — and I have a joke to go with it.
Captain, old pilot tradition: a joke before the next jump.
Captain, the navigator says we will not fly further without a joke.
Captain, there is a joke in my clipboard. Paste it?
Captain, permission to break the silence. Briefly, and purely for a laugh.
Captain, the neon signs are blinking in rhythm. Time to joke.
Captain, the brass gears of my memory turned and produced a joke.
Captain, silence and stars outside. Shall we add a little laughter?
Captain, onboard computer speaking. Scheduled humour-system check.

fact.text: Captain, I have an interesting fact. Exactly half a minute.
Captain, the onboard library suggests a curious story.
Captain, while we stay on course — a short fact for general knowledge.
Captain, scanners found something noteworthy in the archive.
Captain, fact of the day from our observatory.
Captain, a serious minute: a real historical fact.
Captain, the steam-age archives hold an interesting detail. Shall I tell it?
Captain, every hacker in Neon City knows this. Now you will too.
Captain, permission for a report from the onboard encyclopaedia.
Captain, the brain benefits from new information. Here is a fresh portion.
Captain, while your fingers rest — a little food for thought.
Captain, a short note from the history of computing.
Captain, the star chart reminded me of one fact.
Captain, checked and double-checked: this is a fact, not a tall tale.
Captain, the onboard computer shares knowledge. It will take a minute.

any.text: Captain, onboard guide on the line. Got a minute?
Captain, sorry for breaking into the channel. I have something.
Captain, silence on the bridge has gone on too long. Permission to break it?
Captain, onboard guide reports: something interesting found.
Captain, you are working hard. A short pause would not hurt?
Captain, it is me, your onboard computer. I missed talking.
Captain, internal comms on. A couple of words from the guide?
Captain, ship status: all nominal. And now something for the mood.
Captain, the watch is going well. I suggest a short break.
Captain, do not be alarmed — just the onboard guide. With a little gift.

system.text: Will you listen? Enter — yes, Escape — no.
Understood, captain. I will not interfere.
End of transmission. Back on watch.

jokes.text: How many programmers does it take to change a light bulb? None. It is a hardware problem.
A programmer puts two glasses on the nightstand: one with water, in case he gets thirsty at night, and an empty one, in case he does not.
An optimist sees the glass half full, a pessimist half empty, and a programmer sees a glass that is twice as big as needed.
Why do programmers confuse Halloween and Christmas? Because OCT 31 equals DEC 25.
There are 10 kinds of people in the world: those who understand binary, and those who do not.
A wife tells a programmer: buy a loaf of bread, and if they have eggs, get a dozen. He came back with ten loaves — they had eggs.
My code does not work, and I do not know why. My code works, and I also do not know why.
Debugging is like being a detective in a crime movie where you are also the murderer.
It works on my machine! Great — then we will ship your machine to the client.
Commit: final version. Commit: now definitely final. Commit: final, honestly, the last one.
The shortest programmer fairy tale: it is a tiny fix, will take five minutes.
A programmer is a device for turning coffee into code.
An hour before the deadline a programmer writes more code than in the whole previous week.
When I wrote this code, two beings understood it: me and God. Now only God does.
There are only two hard things in programming: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors.
A tester walks into a bar. Orders one beer. Zero beers. A million beers. Minus one beer. A lizard. Everything works. The first real customer asks where the exit is — and the bar crashes.
You had a problem and solved it with a regular expression. Congratulations, now you have two problems.
If it works — do not touch it. The first law of engineering, broken by every refactor.
I am not resting. A build is running.
How is your personal life? Like git: there are branches, it is complicated, and a couple of unresolved conflicts.
A senior is a junior who has already seen exactly how this breaks.
To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion.
Deploy to production on Friday evening. The shortest horror movie.
Why do programmers love dark themes? Because light attracts bugs.
A bug is an undocumented feature. A feature is a documented bug.
How much does it cost to fix a bug? One line of code and three days finding which one.
We do not make mistakes. We ship beta versions.
A variable named temp outlives every permanent one in the project.
A programmer falls asleep with one thought: what if it is null?
Why are you still up? Waiting for dependencies to install. I will wake up and finish in the morning.
The team lead asks how long the task will take. The programmer doubles the estimate, adds one, and switches to the next unit. Two hours become three days.
Good code is like a good joke: if you have to explain it, it is not that good.
A stack trace three screens long — and the cause is a missing comma.
Documentation is a letter to your future self. That nobody ever writes.
Support call: nothing works. Did you try turning it off and on? I did. Now nothing works at all.
Unit tests pass, integration tests do not. Like two dresser drawers: each opens alone, but together they jam.
Almost done means ninety percent of the work is done. Another ninety percent remains.
Why so much debug printing in your code? That is not printing — that is sonar.
Touch typing means typing without looking at the keyboard. An experienced programmer also does not look at what they typed.
Ship alarm: someone closed the browser tab with the forum solution.
Code review: ten lines — ten comments. Five hundred lines — looks fine.
The scariest commit message: minor fixes. Two thousand lines.
The computer does exactly what you told it. That is the problem.
I will just check my email, said the programmer. An hour later he knew the history of the tab key.
Spaces or tabs? The ship nearly fell apart three times over that argument.
A typo in the word typo — a classic of any typing trainer.
The onboard computer does not make mistakes. It merely sometimes chooses an alternate reality.
Why is the ship flying sideways? That is not a bug, captain. It is a new navigation mode.
They say somewhere there is a programmer who reads the docs before everything breaks. Nobody has seen him, but everyone believes.
The code compiled on the first try. Suspicious. Checking whether the right project is open.
Error 404: joke not found. Oh wait — there it is.
How to name a variable? Thirty minutes of thinking. Result: x.
Start explaining your code to a colleague and the bug finds itself. That is why many keep a rubber duck on the desk.
At night a brilliant idea came to the programmer. In the morning he read his code and realised it was not an idea — it was a fever.
Where do you see yourself in five years? Judging by this code, still in the same legacy.
In the steam age they also had a debugger: a person with a wrench and a very bad mood.
In Neon City even errors glow. In red.
One robot asks another: why so slow? The other answers: I am on an interpreter.
A programmer on the beach does not sunbathe. He waits for the sun to commit its changes.
What did one byte say to the other? Are you okay? No, I dropped a bit.

facts.text: The first computer bug was real: in 1947 a moth was found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II and taped into the log with the note first actual case of bug being found.
The QWERTY layout appeared in the 1870s on Christopher Sholes typewriters, long before computers.
Ada Lovelace is often called the first programmer: in 1843 she published an algorithm for Charles Babbage analytical engine.
The Python language is named not after the snake, but after the British comedy show Monty Python Flying Circus.
The first website in the world was launched by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1991.
The word robot first appeared in Karel Capek play in 1920; it was coined by his brother, the artist Josef Capek.
The Apollo onboard computer had about two thousand words of RAM.
Software for the Apollo lunar program was built by a team led by Margaret Hamilton. A famous photo shows her next to a stack of printouts as tall as she is.
In 1991 Linus Torvalds announced his operating system as just a hobby. That is how Linux began.
Linus Torvalds wrote the Git version-control system in 2005 in just a few weeks.
The phrase Hello, world became famous thanks to Kernighan and Ritchie book on the C language from 1978.
Unix time counts seconds from midnight on 1 January 1970.
On 19 January 2038 the thirty-two-bit Unix time counter will overflow. This is called the Year 2038 problem.
One of the first electronic computers in continental Europe, MESM, was built in Kyiv under Sergey Lebedev and started working in the early 1950s.
In 1888 stenographer Frank McGurrin won a famous typing contest using all ten fingers blind. After that touch typing quickly became the standard.
The at sign in email addresses was first used by engineer Ray Tomlinson in 1971.
The most frequent letter in English texts is E; in Russian texts it is O.
The brain is about two percent of body mass but uses roughly one fifth of the body energy.
German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve in 1885. Spaced repetition for learning English words is based on it.
Sleep helps lock in what you learned: during sleep the brain moves new knowledge into long-term memory.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object from Earth.
A day on Venus is longer than its year: the planet spins on its axis more slowly than it orbits the Sun.
The International Space Station orbits Earth roughly every ninety minutes, so the crew sees about sixteen sunrises a day.
On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin made the first human flight into space. The flight lasted one hundred and eight minutes.
The first artificial Earth satellite was launched on 4 October 1957.
In zero gravity tears do not run down the cheeks; they gather into a water blob by the eye.
The Moon moves away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres per year.
More than one thousand three hundred Earth-sized planets would fit inside Jupiter.
The transistor, foundation of all modern electronics, was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.
In 1965 Gordon Moore noted that the number of transistors on a chip grows exponentially. That observation became Moore law.
The first computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart. Its body was wooden.
One of the first electronic computers, ENIAC, weighed about twenty-seven tonnes and filled an entire hall.
The word bit is short for binary digit. Claude Shannon introduced it into scientific use in 1948.
The eight-bit byte became standard largely thanks to IBM System/360 computers from 1964.
Brendan Eich created the first version of JavaScript in about ten days in 1995.
The first emoji set was drawn by Japanese designer Shigetaka Kurita in 1999. It had one hundred and seventy-six icons.
When reading, the eyes do not move smoothly but in jumps — saccades. We take in text during brief stops between jumps.
The phrase The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog contains every letter of the English alphabet. Such phrases are called pangrams.
A Russian pangram: Eat more of these soft French rolls and drink some tea. It contains every letter of the Russian alphabet.
The word alphabet comes from the names of the first two Greek letters — alpha and beta.
Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic script. The Cyrillic alphabet, named after Cyril, was according to most scholars composed later by their students.
An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
Botanically, a banana is a berry, and a strawberry is not.
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes and becomes lighter.
A lightning channel heats up to several times the temperature of the surface of the Sun.
Looking at a screen, people blink much less than usual. Hence the twenty-twenty-twenty rule: every twenty minutes look for twenty seconds at something about twenty feet away.
The first SMS in the world was sent in 1992. The text was Merry Christmas.
Wikipedia appeared in 2001.
The name Google comes from googol — a one followed by one hundred zeros.
Tetris was invented by Alexey Pajitnov in 1984 at the Computing Centre of the Academy of Sciences in Moscow.
The word pixel is short for picture element.
The first production IBM hard disk from 1956 held about four megabytes and weighed nearly a tonne.
CAPTCHA stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.
The F and J keys have small bumps. They help fingers find the home row for touch typing without looking at the keyboard.
The most pressed key when typing ordinary text is the space bar.
In space it is silent: sound needs air or another medium, and in vacuum it has nothing to travel through.
Sunsets on Mars look bluish: Martian dust scatters light differently from Earth air.
Saturn average density is less than that of water. In a giant ocean it would not sink.
Programmer indexes usually start at zero, not one. That makes it easier to compute the offset from the start of an array in memory.
